Sufficient supply especially of food or fuel
Gradual choking especially from smoke or fumes
days.r: Late Latin sufferentia: suffer + -ance
days.s: When his talk trespasses beyond sufferance, I chastise him.

days.d: Marked by up-to-dateness in dress and manners
f: Marked by thick tufts of coarse hair
Marked by a fondness for lotteries and games of chance
Marked by a dry, rasping cough
days.r: Raff “persons of the lowest class” + -ish; compare riffraff
days.s: The smokers' most raffish outsider, Comstock, appeared to do nothing but smoke.

days.d: More than is needed, desired, or required

Fond of asking endless questions
Guided by a belief in the supernatural

days.s: It is, for example, not clear whether “love thy enemy” is a precept or a supererogatory counsel.

days.d: Formal expression of respect
f: Formal ending of a marriage
Formal renunciation of faith
Formal request for payment
days.r: Old French deveir, from Latin dēbēre “to owe; ought, must”
days.s: I should have long ere this paid my devoirs to the inhabitants of Raymond Castle.

days.d: Consider carefully and deeply; reflect upon; turn over in one’s mind

Grow thick; turn from a liquid into a soft jelly or solid
Cut away; remove the outer layer of bark from a tree trunk
days.r: Latin cōgitō “to think”
days.s: Think, ladies! Cogitate! Sharpen up the edges of your wit.

days.d: A club that is used as a weapon
f: A hug that is given to a child
A fool that is easily tricked
A cup that is used for ale

days.s: The guard hefted his cudgel menacingly and looked at the inmates.

days.d: Detrimental to health
f: Lacking in salt
Indecent and lewd
Lacking a greeting
days.r: In- + salubrious
days.s: For the most part London's traditional areas were overcrowded and insalubrious.

A deep sleep caused by a fever
A formal list of goods for sale
days.r: Greek katáphraktos “suit of armour”, from kata- + phraktós “protected; fenced in”
days.s: Carmine streaks stained their limbs, their tunics and cataphracts; but little of the blood was theirs.

days.d: Narcotic consisting of an alcohol solution of opium or any preparation in which opium is the main ingredient
f: Hymn consisting of a short verse of praise or any song in which the name of God is repeated
Ointment consisting of a mixture of wax and herbs or any salve in which lanolin is the main ingredient
Perfume consisting of a distillation of lavender or any essence in which the flower oil is the main ingredient
days.r: New Latin, from lādanum “a gum resin”, from Greek lā́danon; used by Paracelsus
days.s: Whipping and abuse are like laudanum; you have to double the dose as the sensibilities decline.

days.d: The intellectual conception of a thing as it is in itself, not as it is known through perception

The heavenly light of a saint as it is painted in an icon, not as it is described in scripture
The numerical value of a letter as it is used in counting, not as it is spoken aloud
days.r: German Noumenon, from Greek nooúmenon “thing that is known”, from noéō “I know”
days.s: That, we have seen, is what prevents the two truths from collapsing into an appearance/reality or phenomenon/noumenon distinction.

days.d: Produce a literary work
f: Stir up trouble
Point out clearly
Mark with a dent
days.r: Old French enditer, from Late Latin indictāre; a doublet of indict
days.s: My heart is inditing a good matter.

days.d: A decorative musical accompaniment (often improvised) added above a basic melody
f: A gradual slope (often gentle) leading down from the top of a hill to a valley floor
A low murmuring chant (often repeated) sung beneath the main melody by the basses
A small sharp tool (often curved) used by surgeons to cut away diseased tissue
days.r: Anglo-Norman descaunt, from Medieval Latin discantus; a doublet of discant
days.s: Upon that simplest of themes how magnificent a descant!

days.d: Something unspecified whose name is either forgotten or not known
f: Something small and round that is fried in fat and eaten with fish
Someone foolish and gullible who is easily tricked out of money
Something thick and lumpy that is used to fill cracks in walls
days.r: Gobbin “piece, portion, slice”, from Anglo-Norman gobon; before 1553
days.s: I always have a plethora of extra gubbins I can't remember.
